Since the HTTP web server is the foundation's original project, Apache played a key role in the initial growth of the World Wide Web. Apache has become, and has remained the most popular web server software since April 1996.
In 2009, it became the first web server software to serve more than 100 million websites, and in 2016, it serves roughly 45 percent of all active websites in the world.
Because of this popularity, Apache benefits from great documentation and integrated support from other software projects.
Connection Handling
To handle connections, Apache has a variety of multi-processing modules called MPMs. These modules dictate how requests should be handled, and allows administrators to set up its connection handling architecture.
The MPMs include: mpm_prefork, mpm_worker and mpm_event.
Serving Contents
Apache handles static contents using its conventional file-based methods. For dynamic contents, it embeds a processor of the language the content uses, into its workers. This allows Apache to execute dynamic contents straight within itself without having to rely on external processor or components.
Its ability to handle both static and dynamic contents internally means that the setup and configuration is simpler to Nginx.
Configuration
Apache has an option to allow additional or customized configuration per-directory level. These are done using files known as .htaccess.
Residing inside directories, Apache will first check for the files' existence before serving any contents. If a .htaccess file is found, Apache will apply the directives within, to the path where the file exists. This allows Apache to run a decentralized configuration, away from the web server's default configuration.
By having the ability to understand directory-level configurations, Apache is more flexible if compared to Nginx. For certain web software, like Content Management Systems (CMS) for example, administrators can configure certain parts of the website behave from its server's path.
Interpreting Requests
Apache has the ability to interpret a request as a physical resource on the filesystem or as a URI location. For example, Apache can use , and blocks.
For Apache, the default to interpret requests is to have process them as filesystem resources. Because Apache was designed and built from ground up as a web server, it begins by taking the root of a document to then append the portion of the request following the host and the port number in order to find what it is looking for.
Here, Apache's filesystem hierarchy is represented as a document tree.
When a request doesn't match the underlying filesystem, Apache can use the Alias directive to map the request to an alternative location. Using the blocks, Apache can work using the URI itself instead of the filesystem.
Modules
Apache's modules can be loaded or unloaded dynamically. While the Apache's core is always on, additional functionality using modules can be turned on or off in the running server by hooking them into the main server.

Question: How does Apache handle dynamic content? Answer: It embeds a processor of the language the content uses into its workers, allowing it to execute dynamic content internally.

Question: What was the first milestone Apache achieved in terms of the number of websites served? Answer: It became the first web server software to serve more than 100 million websites in 2009.

Chapter 1 Introduction

High power microwave generation has been an important and fascinating field of research for a long time. At microwave frequencies one employs conventional microwave devices like klystron, magnetron and travelling wave tubes (TWT) for the generation of high powers at 1-30 cm of wavelength. These conventional microwave devices employ non-relativistic electron beams to generate microwaves at wavelengths > 1cm with high efficiency. In a two cavity klystron [22] the electron beam is modulated in the buncher cavity by the radiation field (rf) resulting in density modulation of the electrons as they travel towards the catcher cavity. When the electron bunches pass through the alternating field of the catcher cavity during its retarding phase, the electrons transfer energy to the rf field. A feedback from the catcher to buncher gives rise to oscillations. In a magnetron, an electron moves in crossed electric and magnetic field following a spiral path. When a rf field is applied to the anode circuit, those electrons entering the circuit during the retarding field are decelerated and give up energy to the rf field. Those electrons entering the circuit during the accelerating field are accelerated and are returned back towards the cathode. A traveling wave tube (TWT) uses a slow wave structure to slow down the phase velocity of an electromagnetic wave to less than c, the velocity of light. An electron beam with velocity \( v_b \) equal to the phase velocity of an electromagnetic wave efficiently interacts with the wave. For \( v_b \) slightly greater than the phase velocity of the wave the electrons are bunched in the retarding phase of the wave so
that they can give energy to the wave resulting in an exponential growth of the wave. However, these devices cannot be operated at wavelengths below a centimeter. Conventional lasers can be used at wavelengths $\lambda \leq 10\mu m$, however, the output frequency strictly depends on the atomic structure and cannot be controlled by the external parameters. Further the efficiency of lasers is quite poor.

Figure 1.1 Peak power (in watts) of various high-Powered Sources of Coherent Radiation at centimeter to submicron wavelengths ($\lambda$) [32].
The quest for the generation of high power coherent radiation at millimeter, sub-millimeter and shorter wavelengths has led to the significant improvement and development of several microwave devices, e.g., Free electron lasers, Cerenkov Free electron lasers and gyrotron, due to the availability of intense relativistic electron beam (IREB), which has increased the ability to model complicated structures and understanding their properties. Figure 1.1 gives peak power (in watts) of various high power sources of coherent radiation at centimeter to submicron wavelengths. One may note that the free electron laser operates over a wide frequency range and has promise for much shorter wavelengths.

All these microwave devices involve resonant transfer of energy from a beam of electrons to a radiation signal resulting in its amplification. For the resonant transfer of energy from a beam of electrons, the phase synchronism conditions, i.e., the energy and momentum conservation conditions should be simultaneously satisfied. Depending on the way in which phase synchronism is achieved these microwave devices are classified in three categories.

1.1 Types of Microwave Devices

1.1.1 Slow Wave Devices

These devices involve the interaction of relativistic electron beam propagating along the axis of a slow wave structure with the electromagnetic wave having the phase velocity slightly less than the beam velocity due to slow wave structure. Travelling wave tubes (TWTs) and Cerenkov Free electron laser (CFEL) are the examples of this category.
1.1.2 Fast Wave Devices

These devices involve the interaction between the gyrating electrons and the natural mode of the cavity having phase velocity larger than "c", i.e. speed of light in free space. Gyrotron and cyclotron auto-resonance masers (CARMS) are two such devices.

1.1.3 Parametric Devices

These devices involve the interaction of an energetic electron beam with a high frequency electromagnetic signal, in the presence of pump wave, called a wiggler. The pump wave may be either an electromagnetic wave or static periodic electric or magnetic field. This interaction mechanism can be explained by two wave or three wave parametric processes depending on the beam current. In two wave parametric process the pump wave and the high frequency electromagnetic wave exerts a non-linear ponderomotive force on the beam electrons to derive the low frequency mode. In this process the amplitude of the high frequency mode grows with time. This process is appropriate for a low density electron beam in which a single particle can be used to describe the interaction. This is called the Compton regime. For high density electron beams the collective effects are important and negative beam space charge wave can participate in a three wave interaction. This is called the Raman regime. Free electron lasers and optical klystron are two popular devices of this category.

In the recent years, free electron lasers (FELs) and Cerenkov free electron lasers (CFELs) have become attractive devices at millimeter to infrared wavelengths and are capable of generating even much shorter wavelengths, up to X-rays. Extensive research work has been
done on free electron laser and Cerenkov free electron laser. FEL experiments at MIT have
been performed by Hartemann et al. [10] in the amplifier mode. An electron beam (175KV, 1-
9KA) with energy spread 0.3% was used. The FEL operated in the frequency range 7-21 GHz,
with a gain of 20dB and efficiency of 12%.

Today, the major concern in the area of high power microwave generation, more
specifically FELs and CFELs is to achieve higher output power levels, i.e., higher efficiencies at
higher operating frequencies. In order to achieve higher output power levels, the main
approach taken is the use of pre-bunched relativistic electron beam. A high power microwave
FEL [40] experiment has been performed to study the inherent electron beam bunching that
occurs in FEL interaction. If one employs a relativistic electron beam already pre-bunched or
pre-modulated at appropriate frequency and wave number, then the efficiency and power
output of the device are expected to be significantly increased. The idea of pre-bunching has
been mooted by the experiment performed by Satio et al. [36], (in KEK Japan). In this case, a
pre-bunched FEL amplifier consisting of a pre-buncher and standard FEL has been designed
and constructed. The saturation power of 120MW has been attained at the wiggler length of
1.1meter by 1.5MeV pre-bunched electron beam with a 45% modulated DC 750A current.
However FEL performances were deteriorated by the beam losses in the wiggler.

The thesis proposes to investigate and analyse the effect of beam pre-bunching on gain
and efficiency in high power microwave devices, more specifically in FEL and CFEL and the
contributions of this present thesis are aimed at efficiency enhancement of FEL and CFEL and
use of alternate wigglers for designing high frequency FELs.
As the coupling of an electromagnetic radiation with an electron beam in microwave devices is very closely related to the issues such as efficiency, frequency, bandwidth and gain, hence the precise knowledge of interaction mechanism and the phase synchronism conditions is required. A brief discussion of the basic interaction mechanism and phase synchronism condition for the devices with which we are concerned, viz., CFEL and FEL is given.

1.2 Cerenkov Free Electron Laser (CFEL)

A Cerenkov free electron laser (CFEL) employs a slow wave medium to slow down the phase velocity of transverse electric (TE) or transverse magnetic (TM) modes to less than c, the velocity of light so that they can be excited by a moderately relativistic electron beam by the process of Cerenkov emission. Ginzburg in 1947 first introduced the idea of cerenkov interaction. Later in 1977, Walsh et al. [15] performed the first Cerenkov maser experiment at Columbia University. They produced millimeter waves at 1MW powers at frequencies 30-60 GHz.

A Cerenkov free electron laser [21] generally employs two kinds of slow wave structures:

1. A dielectric whose dielectric constant is $\varepsilon > 1$ reduces the phase velocity of the radiation wave below c. A moderately relativistic electron beam can excite the electromagnetic radiation by cerenkov emission. Such a device is popularly known as dielectric cerenkov maser.

2. A plasma lining having a dielectric constant $\varepsilon$ given by
\[ \varepsilon = 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}, \]

where \( \omega_p \) is the plasma frequency and \( \omega \) is the radiation frequency, can act as a slowing down medium for \( \omega_p >> \omega \) so that \( |\varepsilon| >> 1 \).

Cerenkov masers employing a combination of plasma and dielectric have also been used.

It consists of an electron accelerator (a Marx generator) which provides a solid cylindrical electron beam of current > 1A and beam voltage 0.5MV. The beam enters the dielectric–lined cylindrical waveguide, where the interaction with electromagnetic wave occurs.

The key element of generation of coherent radiation is the bunching of the electron beam by the radiation field such that electrons are decelerated by the field emitting coherent radiation. The bunching is achieved through phase synchronism. To understand this, consider a relativistic electron beam propagating through a dielectric loaded waveguide with the velocity \( v_b \) parallel \( \hat{z} \). The waveguide supports a TM mode whose electric field has a z-component given as

E_z = A_0 e^{-i(\omega t - kz)}
\]

Case I: When \( v_b \sim \frac{\omega}{k} \), beam velocity is almost equal to the phase velocity of electromagnetic wave, then to the relativistic electrons, the EM wave appears as a static field which can accelerate or decelerate them. If the beam velocity exactly equals the phase velocity of the EM wave, no net transfer of energy takes place as an equal number of electrons, which are initially randomly distributed in phase, are accelerated and decelerated.
Case II: When $v_b < \frac{\omega}{k}$, beam velocity is slightly less than the phase velocity of the wave, electrons are bunched in the accelerating phase of the wave resulting in an increase in their kinetic energy at the expense of the wave amplitude.

Case III: When $v_b > \frac{\omega}{k}$, beam velocity is slightly greater than the phase velocity of the wave, one may view the interaction in a frame moving with the phase velocity of the wave.         return f"Category(name={self.name}, logo={self.logo})"


class CategoryManager:
    """
    Manages a collection of categories.
    
    Methods:
        add_category(name: str, logo: str = 'tour') -> None: Adds a new category.
        update_category(name: str, new_logo: str) -> bool: Updates the logo of an existing category.
        get_category(name: str) -> Optional[Category]: Retrieves a category by name.
        list_categories() -> List[Category]: Lists all categories.
    """
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.categories: List[Category] = []

    def add_category(self, name: str, logo: str = 'tour') -> None:
        """
        Adds a new category to the manager.
        
        Args:
            name (str): The name of the category.
            logo (str): The logo associated with the category, defaulting to 'tour'.
        """
        if any(category.name == name for category in self.categories):
            raise ValueError(f"Category with name '{name}' already exists.")
        self.categories.append(Category(name, logo))

    def update_category(self, name: str, new_logo: str) -> bool:
        """
        Updates the logo of an existing category.
        
        Args:
            name (str): The name of the category to update.
            new_logo (str): The new logo for the category.
            
        Returns:
            bool: True if the category was updated, False otherwise.
        """
        for category in self.categories:
            if category.name == name:
                category.logo = new_logo
                return True
        return False

    def get_category(self, name: str) -> Optional[Category]:
        """
        Retrieves a category by name.
        
        Args:
            name (str): The name of the category to retrieve.
            
        Returns:
            Optional[Category]: The category if found, None otherwise.
        """
        for category in self.categories:
            if category.name == name:
                return category
        return None

    def list_categories(self) -> List[Category]:
        """
        Lists all categories.
        
        Returns:
            List[Category]: A list of all categories.
        """
        return self.categories


def main():
    # Create a category manager instance
    category_manager = CategoryManager()
    
    # Add some categories
    category_manager.add_category("Technology")
    category_manager.add_category("Health", "health-logo")
    category_manager.add_category("Finance", "finance-logo")
    
    # Update a category's logo
    category_manager.update_category("Health", "new-health-logo")
    
    # Retrieve a category
    health_category = category_manager.get_category("Health")
    print(f"Retrieved Category: {health_category}")
    
    # List all categories
    print("\nAll Categories:")
    for category in category_manager.list_categories():
        print(category)

def calculate_strange_counter_value(time: int) -> int:
    """
    Calculate the value of the strange counter at a given time.

    The strange counter starts at a high value and decrements until it reaches 1,
    then resets to a higher value. The pattern follows a specific cycle where each
    cycle's start value is three times the previous cycle's start value.

    Args:
        time (int): The time at which to calculate the strange counter value.

    Returns:
        int: The value of the strange counter at the specified time.
    """
    if time < 0:
        raise ValueError("Time must be a non-negative integer.")

    cycle_index = 0
    current_cycle_start = 3  # Initial start value for the first cycle

    # Determine the cycle in which the given time falls
    while time >= current_cycle_start:
        cycle_index += 1
        current_cycle_start *= 2  # Each subsequent cycle starts at double the previous cycle's start value

    # Calculate the length of the current cycle
    cycle_length = current_cycle_start // 2

    # Calculate the position within the current cycle
    position_within_cycle = time - (current_cycle_start // 2) + 1

    # Calculate the counter value at the given time
    counter_value = cycle_length - position_within_cycle + 1

    return counter_value

To add measurements with different units, follow these steps:

### **Example 1: Adding Meters, Decimeters, Centimeters, and Millimeters**
**Problem:**  
Add 6 m 7 dm 2 cm 5 mm, 8 m 8 dm 6 cm 6 mm, and 10 m 5 mm.  

**Solution:**  
1. **Convert all units to meters** (base unit):  
   - **6 m 7 dm 2 cm 5 mm**  
     - 7 dm = 0.7 m  
     - 2 cm = 0.02 m  
     - 5 mm = 0.005 m  
     - Total: $6 + 0.7 + 0.02 + 0.005 = 6.725$ m  
   - **8 m 8 dm 6 cm 6 mm**  
     - 8 dm = 0.8 m  
     - 6 cm = 0.06 m  
     - 6 mm = 0.006 m  
     - Total: $8 + 0.8 + 0.06 + 0.006 = 8.866$ m  
   - **10 m 5 mm**  
     - 5 mm = 0.005 m  
     - Total: $10 + 0.005 = 10.005$ m  

2. **Add the decimal values:**  
   $$
   6.725 + 8.866 + 10.005 = 25.596 \, \text{m}
   $$  

**Answer:** $25.596$ meters.  

---

### **Example 2: Adding Grams, Decigrams, Centigrams, and Milligrams**
**Problem:**  
Add 5 g 6 dg 8 cg 4 mg, 15 g 7 mg, 6 dg 5 mg, and 8 g 7 cg 2 mg.  

**Solution:**  
1. **Convert all units to grams** (base unit):  
   - **5 g 6 dg 8 cg 4 mg**  
     - 6 dg = 0.6 g  
     - 8 cg = 0.08 g  
     - 4 mg = 0.004 g  
     - Total: $5 + 0.6 + 0.08 + 0.004 = 5.684$ g  
   - **15 g 7 mg**  
     - 7 mg = 0.007 g  
     - Total: $15 + 0.007 = 15.007$ g  
   - **6 dg 5 mg**  
     - 6 dg = 0.6 g  
     - 5 mg = 0.005 g  
     - Total: $0.6 + 0.005 = 0.605$ g  
   - **8 g 7 cg 2 mg**  
     - 7 cg = 0.07 g  
     - 2 mg = 0.002 g  
     - Total: $8 + 0.07 + 0.002 = 8.072$ g  

2. **Add the decimal values:**  
   $$
   5.684 + 15.007 + 0.605 + 8.072 = 29.368 \, \text{g}
   $$  

**Answer:** $29.368$ grams.  

---

### **Key Steps for Adding Measurements**
1. **Convert all units to a common base unit** (e.g., meters, grams).  
2. **Use decimal equivalents** for smaller units (e.g., 1 dm = 0.1 m, 1 cg = 0.01 g).  
3. **Align decimal points** and add as regular decimals.  
4. **Verify unit compatibility**: Only add measurements of the same dimension (e.g., length + length).  

By following this method, you ensure accurate results when summing mixed-unit measurements.

Filmmaker: Stefan Eling
Country: Germany
Year Made: 2007
Length: 5′ 07″
Technique: hand drawn

From an oblique high angle we see a red-haired man standing in a room. The furniture includes a coffee table, a standard lamp, and a carpet with a spotted pattern. The man switches on the standard lamp and we can see that in the middle of the carpet is a large cube covered with a cloth, on which stand a cup and saucer. He moves the cup and saucer to the coffee table and folds up the cloth. The cube opens to form a chunky armchair, in which he sits, having taken off his slippers. Immediately, a different reality takes over the cube of space directly above the carpet. Rapid piano music begins, his hair flies back as if in a wind, the coffee table, cup, slippers and lamp all vanish behind him, and he seems to be rushing along a road, sitting in the armchair. A number of large eggs fly past him, until he is distracted by a toaster flashing by and one of the eggs hits him in the face. He crashes to the floor and all the objects return to their normal places.

He gets up slowly and gets back into the armchair. The ‘ride’ is again a road, but the chair turns into a low-slung trolley. He passes a traffic light. Suddenly the road changes to a railway track and the trolley into a freight truck. As arrows start to fly past him from behind, the railway changes to sandy ground scattered with skulls and cacti. The truck changes into a chunky wooden horse and a number of cowboy hats flash past. Then a sombrero hits him in the face and he crashes back into his room. There is a toaster on the coffee table instead of the cup and saucer.

The third ride begins as before but quickly everything vanishes and he finds himself in a plane with clouds and birds flying past. Two toasters also fly past and he shows some skill in manoeuvring past these hazards. But then a cup and saucer start to overtake him from behind: looking at this, he collides with a bird and crashes to the floor once more. The cup and saucer are back on the coffee table but a cactus has replaced the standard lamp, and he notices that his slippers have moved to a different part of the room.

In the fourth ride, the chair drives straight into the sea and changes into a boat. He negotiates posts and lifebelts in the sea before a huge wave rolls over him, the boat changes to an underwater jet ski and he acquires goggles and breathing apparatus. He negotiates many different fish but fails to notice a figure just like himself lying on the floor as he has done after each crash, although facing in the opposite direction. A shark swims alongside and bites off his breathing apparatus. Back in the living room, the coffee table has gone and a traffic light and railway signal unit have appeared.

In the fifth ride, the chair quickly changes to a trolley and then a motorbike. He swerves to avoid hedgehogs and tyres lying in the road, then several other motorcyclists, the coffee table, the standard lamp, the spotted carpet and his slippers. Finally he crashes headlong into another motorcyclist and disappears. The chair is now facing in the opposite direction, with the motorcyclist lying on the floor in front of it. The motorcyclist – who seems to be a pig – gets up, puts on the slippers, replaces the cover on the folded-up armchair and the cup and saucer on top of it, and switches off the standard lamp

Filmmaker’s comments

My main inspiration was that so many men waste their time with computer games. My ideas for the film were: that it would be funnier if we could change the shape of the furniture in our living rooms, rather than buy small ugly games consoles; to mix a modern visual theme with traditional 2D drawn animation that has a 3D ‘look’ and to use classical piano music; to bring action and motion to what is normally a quiet place: an ordinary carpeted living room; that it would be interesting to have a ‘virtual enemy’ take over at the end and wear my slippers! The difficult part was finding the time to do all the hand drawings that make up the film when I had to earn my living doing other things.

Things you might notice

The ‘camera position’ never changes; and you could consider the effect of having a high-angle, oblique shot. What if the audience’s point of view were different, or if there were several different viewpoints as in most films?
The colour range is very limited, brightening up only in the game world. • We don’t know anything else about this man apart from the things he has in his living room and what he does in it – or where he goes at the end.
The effect of the music (try showing the film without the music, or playing the music on its own before showing
the film).

Themes to explore

‘Ride’ type computer games – why are they such fun? What makes them addictive? Which are the best ones (and why)? Do some children prefer them to other types of game (eg shoot-em up, quest, virtual worlds) – why/why not? Are there ‘rules’ in some families about how much time to spend on them? (If so, why, and do children keep to them?) Do boys like them more than girls? (If so, why?) Do children ever worry that they are spending too much time playing games? If they could invent a ‘ride’ game what would it be like?
What’s real and what isn’t in this film? This is a complex question but children can enjoy exploring and reflecting on the criteria they use when judging something as ‘real’. For example a ride is more exciting if it is realistic: you may believe it is real while you are playing. Watch out for the ways in which Eling signals the switches between the ordinary everyday world and the game world. Look for the objects that appear and disappear, passing through the ‘cube’ of the game world: which ones originate in the living room and which ones come from the game world?
An impossible ending? The film ends when the central character disappears completely (and for ever?) from the scene and is replaced by a character from the game world. Watch carefully to spot how this happens. You might want to stop the film just before the end, or once the children have grasped the pattern, and ask what they think the ending might be. This could encourage ideas about how to finish off the scenario with a funny and/or meaningful conclusion. Children may also want to discuss “What happens next?” or Cyber 2: does the character from the game world settle down in the living room? Does the film’s central character settle down in the game world – or did he originally come from the game world himself?
Is there a moral to the story? Does Eling want to put us off computer games?

import argparse
import json
import logging
import math
import os
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch
import kaldiio

from torchain import io
from torchain.functions import chain_loss, ChainResults
import models


def get_command_line_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    """
    Parse command-line arguments for training a model.

    Returns:
        argparse.ArgumentParser: Parser object containing all the arguments.
    """
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Train a model using LF-MMI loss.")
    # Paths
    parser.add_argument('--model_dir', required=True, type=str, help='Directory to store model files.')
    parser.add_argument('--den_fst', required=True, type=str, help='Denominator FST file.')
    parser.add_argument('--train_scp', required=True, type=str, help='Training script file.')
    parser.add_argument('--valid_scp', required=True, type=str, help='Validation script file.')
    parser.add_argument('--lda_mat', type=str, default=None, help='LDA matrix file path (optional).')

    # Optimization
    parser.add_argument('--lr', default=1e-3, type=float, help='Learning rate.')
    parser.add_argument('--momentum', default=0.0, type=float, help='Momentum.')
    parser.add_argument('--optimizer', default='SGD', type=str, help='Optimizer name.')
    parser.add_argument('--weight_decay', default=5e-2, type=float, help='Weight decay.')
    parser.add_argument('--l2_regularize', default=5e-5, type=float, help='L2 regularization for LF-MMI.')
    parser.add_argument('--leaky_hmm_coefficient', default=0.1, type=float, help='Leaky HMM coefficient for LF-MMI.')
    parser.add_argument('--xent_regularize', default=0.1, type=float, help='Cross entropy regularization for LF-MMI.')
    parser.add_argument('--train_minibatch_size', default=256, type=int, help='Number of training minibatches.')
    parser.add_argument('--valid_minibatch_size', default=256, type=int, help='Number of validation minibatches.')
    parser.add_argument('--n_epochs', default=10, type=int, help='Number of training epochs.')
    parser.add_argument('--accum_grad', default=1, type=int, help='Number of gradient accumulations before update.')
    parser.add_argument('--no_ivector', action='store_true', help='Disable i-vector usage.')

    # Miscellaneous
    parser.add_argument('--seed', default=777, type=int, help='Random seed.')
    return parser


def configure_logging(parsed_args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    """
    Set up logging with relevant information.

    Args:
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.
    """
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
    logging.info("CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=" + os.environ.get("CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES", ""))
    logging.info("HOST=" + os.environ.get("HOST", ""))
    logging.info("SLURM_JOB_ID=" + os.environ.get("SLURM_JOB_ID", ""))
    logging.info(f"Parsed Arguments: {parsed_args}")


def load_and_prepare_data(parsed_args: argparse.Namespace) -> tuple:
    """
    Load and prepare data for training and validation.

    Args:
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.

    Returns:
        tuple: Training examples, validation examples, number of PDFs, number of features, number of i-vectors.
    """
    io.set_kaldi_device()
    train_examples = io.RandExample(parsed_args.train_scp, parsed_args.seed, parsed_args.train_minibatch_size)
    valid_examples = io.RandExample(parsed_args.valid_scp, parsed_args.seed, parsed_args.valid_minibatch_size)
    logging.info(f"Train set batch: {train_examples.n_batch}, sample: {train_examples.n_data}")
    logging.info(f"Valid set batch: {valid_examples.n_batch}, sample: {valid_examples.n_data}")

    (mfcc, ivec), supervision = valid_examples.value()
    num_pdfs = supervision.n_pdf
    num_features = mfcc.shape[1]
    num_ivectors = ivec.shape[1]
    logging.info(f"Shape info: (num_features: {num_features}, num_ivectors: {num_ivectors}, num_pdfs: {num_pdfs})")
    return train_examples, valid_examples, num_pdfs, num_features, num_ivectors


def load_denominator_fst(parsed_args: argparse.Namespace, num_pdfs: int) -> io.DenominatorGraph:
    """
    Load the denominator FST graph.

    Args:
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.
        num_pdfs (int): Number of PDFs.

    Returns:
        io.DenominatorGraph: Denominator graph object.
    """
    return io.DenominatorGraph(parsed_args.den_fst, num_pdfs)


def load_lda_transformation_matrix(parsed_args: argparse.Namespace) -> torch.Tensor:
    """
    Load the LDA transformation matrix if provided.

    Args:
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.

    Returns:
        torch.Tensor: LDA transformation matrix or None if not provided.
    """
    if parsed_args.lda_mat:
        lda_matrix = kaldiio.load_mat(parsed_args.lda_mat)
        return torch.from_numpy(lda_matrix)
    return None


def initialize_model(parsed_args: argparse.Namespace, num_pdfs: int, num_features: int, num_ivectors: int, lda_matrix: torch.Tensor) -> torch.nn.Module:
    """
    Initialize the model with the given parameters.

    Args:
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.
        num_pdfs (int): Number of PDFs.
        num_features (int): Number of features.
        num_ivectors (int): Number of i-vectors.
        lda_matrix (torch.Tensor): LDA transformation matrix.

    Returns:
        torch.nn.Module: Initialized model.
    """
    model = models.SelfAttentionTDNN(num_pdfs, num_features, num_ivectors, lda_mat=lda_matrix, args=parsed_args)
    model = torch.nn.DataParallel(model)
    model.cuda()
    logging.info(f"Model Architecture:\n{model}")
    return model


def configure_optimizer(parsed_args: argparse.Namespace, model: torch.nn.Module) -> torch.optim.Optimizer:
    """
    Configure the optimizer based on the parsed arguments.

    Args:
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.
        model (torch.nn.Module): Model for which the optimizer is configured.

    Returns:
        torch.optim.Optimizer: Configured optimizer.
    """
    parameters = model.module.kaldi_like_parameters()
    if parsed_args.optimizer == "Nesterov":
        return torch.optim.SGD(parameters, lr=parsed_args.lr, weight_decay=parsed_args.weight_decay, nesterov=True, momentum=parsed_args.momentum)
    optimizer_class = getattr(torch.optim, parsed_args.optimizer)
    optimizer = optimizer_class(parameters, lr=parsed_args.lr, weight_decay=parsed_args.weight_decay)
    for parameter_group in optimizer.param_groups:
        if "momentum" in parameter_group:
            parameter_group["momentum"] = parsed_args.momentum
    return optimizer


def perform_forward_pass(data: tuple, model: torch.nn.Module, den_graph: io.DenominatorGraph, parsed_args: argparse.Namespace) -> tuple:
    """
    Perform a forward pass through the model and compute the loss.

    Args:
        data (tuple): Input data consisting of MFCCs, i-vectors, and supervision.
        model (torch.nn.Module): Model to perform the forward pass.
        den_graph (io.DenominatorGraph): Denominator graph for computing the loss.
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.

    Returns:
        tuple: Loss and results from the forward pass.
    """
    (mfcc, ivec), supervision = data
    batch_size, _, time_steps_in = mfcc.shape
    time_steps_out = math.floor((time_steps_in - (29 - 1) - 1) / 3 + 1)
    lf_mmi_prediction, xe_prediction = model(mfcc.cuda(), ivec.cuda())
    expected_shape = (batch_size, den_graph.n_pdf, time_steps_out)
    assert lf_mmi_prediction.shape == expected_shape, f"Expected shape {expected_shape}, but got {lf_mmi_prediction.shape}"
    return chain_loss(
        lf_mmi_prediction, den_graph, supervision,
        l2_regularize=parsed_args.l2_regularize,
        leaky_hmm_coefficient=parsed_args.leaky_hmm_coefficient,
        xent_regularize=parsed_args.xent_regularize,
        xent_input=xe_prediction, kaldi_way=True
    )


def train_one_epoch(model: torch.nn.Module, optimizer: torch.optim.Optimizer, train_examples, den_graph: io.DenominatorGraph, parsed_args: argparse.Namespace) -> ChainResults:
    """
    Train the model for one epoch.

    Args:
        model (torch.nn.Module): Model to be trained.
        optimizer (torch.optim.Optimizer): Optimizer for updating model weights.
        train_examples: Training data examples.
        den_graph (io.DenominatorGraph): Denominator graph for computing the loss.
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.

    Returns:
        ChainResults: Results from the training epoch.
    """
    model.train()
    train_results = ChainResults()
    train_examples.reset()
    for iteration, data in enumerate(train_examples, start=1):
        loss, results = perform_forward_pass(data, model, den_graph, parsed_args)
        loss.backward()
        if iteration % parsed_args.accum_grad == 0:
            optimizer.step()
            optimizer.zero_grad()
        train_results.data += results.data
        logging.info(f"Train loss: {results}, average: {train_results.loss}, iteration {iteration} / {train_examples.n_batch}")
    logging.info(f"Summary train loss average: {train_results.loss}")
    return train_results


def validate_one_epoch(model: torch.nn.Module, valid_examples, den_graph: io.DenominatorGraph, parsed_args: argparse.Namespace) -> ChainResults:
    """
    Validate the model for one epoch.

    Args:
        model (torch.nn.Module): Model to be validated.
        valid_examples: Validation data examples.
        den_graph (io.DenominatorGraph): Denominator graph for computing the loss.
        parsed_args (argparse.Namespace): Parsed command-line arguments.

    Returns:
        ChainResults: Results from the validation epoch.
    """
    model.eval()
    valid_results = ChainResults()
    valid_examples.reset()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for iteration, data in enumerate(valid_examples, start=1):
            loss, results = perform_forward_pass(data, model, den_graph, parsed_args)
            valid_results.data += results.data
            logging.info(f"Valid loss: {results}, average: {valid_results.loss}, iteration {iteration} / {valid_examples.n_batch}")
    logging.info(f"Summary valid loss average: {valid_results.loss}")
    return valid_results


def main() -> None:
    """
    Main function to execute the training process.
    """
    parsed_arguments = get_command_line_parser().parse_args()
    configure_logging(parsed_arguments)

    model_directory = Path(parsed_arguments.model_dir)
    model_directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with open(model_directory / "args.json", "w") as json_file:
        json.dump(vars(parsed_arguments), json_file, ensure_ascii=False, indent=4)

    torch.manual_seed(parsed_arguments.seed)
    np.random.seed(parsed_arguments.seed)

    train_egs, valid_egs, num_pdfs, num_features, num_ivectors = load_and_prepare_data(parsed_arguments)
    den_graph = load_denominator_fst(parsed_arguments, num_pdfs)
    lda_matrix = load_lda_transformation_matrix(parsed_arguments)

    optimizer = configure_optimizer(parsed_arguments, model)

The end of the Chichester Festival Theatre’s KING LEAR tore my heart out and cast its remnants on a desolate plain. But I’ll get to that later. Up to then, Angus Jackson’s production, currently on loan to BAM, is refreshingly straightforward but somewhat nondescript; it tells the story, without dragging, but rises only occasionally to an emotional or aesthetic height.

Robert Innes Hopkins’ décor is appealingly basic, a few layered platforms against a backdrop of high, straight pillars, all done in shades of brown with accents of mauve, including a pair of side panels in which the colors bleed into each other, as though in a diptych by Rothko (whose spiritual inclinations would be appropriate to the material). When the actors stand tall and taut in the first scene they are as one, compositionally, with the pylons at the rear. On the other hand, there is something about the space that makes the actors hesitate when exiting the stage – perhaps it is too dark to see. This affects the flow of the drama, but visually, at least, everything is of a piece.

The acting itself is variable, from Frank Langella’s Lear on down. Initially, the lead’s presence, augmented by his fame, and the rumble of his voice, makes the other men on stage sound a little squeaky (the women playing Regan and Goneril hold their own). Fortunately, this effect dissipates; in fact, Langella’s attitude toward the ensemble is, by all appearances, generous and supportive. One wonders, even, if he is holding back, for – now I must say it – his Lear is oddly subdued. He does, to be fair, convey the hypocrisy of one who gives up power but still expects that his every desire be fulfilled, and whose temper flairs when they are not. But what is it, really, that leads this man to banish his most loving daughter and behave so fecklessly with the ungrateful two upon whom he blandishes his kingdom? Is his downfall a moral one, as would seem necessary to give meaning to his redemption, or the result of physical and mental decay, such that his condition, rather than what he does, is what is tragic?

Langella goes more with the latter than the former, playing “old” from the start, adding a wobble to his gait and a catch to his voice. Lots of older actors fall into this trap: Langella is 76 and need not play it. If there are particular infirmities to the character, yes, play those, but not the age itself. Highlighting age as the issue could be the point, of course, that Lear is no more than indifferently flawed, just old, that he is, like Job, a fly to the gods, who dutifully swat him, his moral character of no particular relevance. That theme is, indeed, explicitly stated, and redounds on virtually every figure in the drama, whether they are hanged or blinded or dispossessed, and maybe an overemphasis on this explains why we feel so little for so much of this production: even the gouging out of Gloucester’s eyes, realistic though it is, has little impact, on us or the actor playing him.

And so the story is told, in a reasonably involving and never boring way, but one yearns for the volcano that Langella might have been, and wishes there were more to his tragedy than arbitrary injustice. But then he is thrown upon the heath and things start to change; we get not the eruption of the mountain but the flow of the lava. I need not chart its full course; in the end Langella plays the moral condition of his character rather than oldness, and enacts the slippage of voice and body that accompanies the loss of love and friendship. His huge lumbering frame – his arms dangling like an ape’s, his shoulders bent like a question mark, his voice reduced to a bare outtake of air – crumbles finally to the ground, and squeaks out a last plea to the universe. Maybe a pin dropped somewhere. As someone once said of another actor in a towering role, he may not have played Lear perfectly, but there are very few actors who could have played him at all.
